title: Designing Long-Running & Async APIs
summary: Some operations take minutes, not milliseconds — designing an API contract where the response is a "started" acknowledgment, not the actual result.

slides.markdown:
A normal API call assumes the answer is ready within a second or two. But transcoding a video, generating a large report, or running a bulk import can take minutes to hours — holding a connection open that long isn't realistic for either side.

The fix is a contract shift: the API responds immediately with "I started this," hands back a way to check on it later, and the client (or the server) follows up once the real result exists. This topic covers that pattern end to end.

slides.sectionTitle: Why a synchronous request/response contract breaks for operations that take minutes
slides.markdown:
A normal HTTP request assumes the server can produce a full response before the connection's timeout — usually seconds, sometimes up to a minute if you push it. An operation genuinely expected to take minutes or hours (video transcoding, a large data export, training a model) breaks that assumption entirely.

Holding a connection open that long is expensive on both ends: the server ties up a worker/thread for the whole duration instead of freeing it to serve other requests, and the client has to keep a socket open and hope nothing in between — a load balancer, a proxy, a mobile network switch — kills it before completion.

The honest fix isn't a longer timeout; it's changing the API's shape so the response comes back fast, and the actual work happens out of band. That shift is effectively moving the operation onto a message-passing model internally — start it, then get notified or check separately — rather than treating it as one long-lived request.

slides.sectionTitle: The 202-Accepted-plus-status pattern: return a job ID immediately, let the client check progress
slides.markdown:
The standard pattern: `POST /reports` returns `202 Accepted` immediately, with a body containing a job ID and a `Location` header pointing at a status resource, e.g. `Location: /reports/jobs/9931`. The client hasn't gotten its result yet — it's gotten an acknowledgment that the work has started.

`202` specifically communicates "accepted for processing, not yet complete" — distinct from `200`/`201`, which imply the operation already finished. This distinction matters to any client or tooling reading status codes generically.

The client (or another process on its behalf) then checks `GET /reports/jobs/9931` later to find out whether the job is still running, failed, or has a result ready — the next slides cover exactly what that status resource should look like.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: client submits, gets a job ID, polls a status endpoint until done
slides.markdown:
![Sequence diagram of a client polling a job status endpoint from pending to done](assets/async-job-sequence.svg)

The client's first call returns almost instantly with just a job ID — no waiting. Every subsequent call to the status endpoint is cheap and fast, since it's just reading a job's current state, not doing the actual work. Once the state becomes `done`, the response includes where to fetch the real result.

The server-side work (the actual transcoding, report generation) happens entirely outside this request/response cycle, in a background worker the client never talks to directly.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: polling vs webhook-on-completion vs a status stream for notifying the client
slides.markdown:
| | Polling the status endpoint | Webhook on completion | Status stream (SSE/WebSocket) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client complexity | Low — repeat a GET on a timer | Needs a reachable public endpoint (see [webhooks and callback APIs](webhooks-and-callback-apis)) | Needs a held-open connection |
| Latency to notice completion | Depends on poll interval | Near-instant | Near-instant |
| Wasted requests | Yes — most polls return "still running" | None — one call, when it matters | None, but the connection itself has a cost |
| Best fit | Simple clients, no public endpoint available | Server-to-server integrations that can host a callback | A live, connected client (open browser tab, app in foreground) |

**How to decide:** polling is the simplest default and fine for most cases if the job typically finishes in seconds-to-low-minutes. Reach for a webhook when the consumer is another backend system that can host a callback endpoint. Reach for a stream when there's already a live, connected client that would otherwise have to poll anyway.

slides.sectionTitle: Designing the status resource: states, progress, and a result location once done
slides.markdown:
A good status resource needs at minimum: a **state** from a small fixed set (`pending`, `running`, `done`, `failed`), and — once `done` — a **location** for the actual result, usually a URL rather than embedding a potentially huge payload directly in the status response.

For anything that takes more than a few seconds, a **progress** indicator (percent complete, or a step count like "3 of 5") meaningfully improves the experience over a bare "still running," especially for anything a human is watching.

On failure, the state alone isn't enough — the response needs an error reason a client (or a support engineer) can act on, mirroring the same structured-error thinking used for synchronous failures: a machine-readable code plus a human-readable message, not just `"failed": true`.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a job-status endpoint's response shape across pending/running/done/failed
Pitfall: a "long-running" endpoint that's just a synchronous call with a very long timeout
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We'll just set the client and server timeouts to 10 minutes instead of adding a whole job/status pattern — it's simpler."

**Why it's wrong:** a held-open connection for 10 minutes ties up a server worker the entire time (multiplying by concurrent requests, this caps throughput hard), and it's fragile — any load balancer, proxy, or mobile network hiccup in between can silently kill a connection that long before it completes, and the client has no way to resume or check status afterward; it just has to retry the whole operation from scratch.

**Correct model:** return fast with a job reference and let the client check back, even if it feels like "more API surface" than a single long call. The job/status pattern isn't extra complexity for its own sake — it's what makes the operation resumable and resilient to exactly the kind of mid-flight network failure a long synchronous call has no way to recover from.
